The Largescale blackfish Girella punctata exhibits a modest body size relative to other kyphosid fishes inhabiting temperate reef systems. Individuals of this species attain a maximum total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a value that represents the ultimate somatic dimension observed across its range in the northwestern Pacific. Field surveys conducted along the rocky shores of southern Japan have consistently documented that reproductive maturation, as indicated by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis, occurs at a total length of 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters]. This body size at puberty corresponds to a transitional life stage where energetic resources that previously supported somatic growth are increasingly directed toward reproductive tissue development. The relationship between length and body mass in this species follows an allometric scaling pattern typical of compressed-bodied perciform fishes, with the weight at sexual maturity estimated from length-weight regressions to be approximately 1,460 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,460 grams]. These morphometric benchmarks are critical for fisheries management, as they define the size window within which individuals should be allowed to mature before harvest.

Reproductive output in Girella punctata is characterized by a moderately high fecundity that reflects its pelagic spawning strategy and broadcast fertilization mode. During the peak spawning season, which coincides with elevated water temperatures in late spring and early summer, females produce an average of 921 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 921 eggs per spawning event], with each female completing approximately 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events per year] at a water temperature of 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C]. This thermal optimum represents the temperature at which oocyte development proceeds most efficiently without inducing thermal stress, reflecting the species' adaptation to the warm Kuroshio Current-influenced waters that characterize its southern range.

Early life history in the Largescale blackfish begins with the production of small, pelagic eggs that measure approximately 1.2 millimeters in diameter, a dimension that is consistent with the eggs of other coastal kyphosids that rely on planktonic larval dispersal. From this egg diameter, the wet weight at birth is calculated to be roughly 0.0009 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0009 grams], a value that represents the mass of the freshly hatched yolk-sac larva immediately following eclosion. At this minute size, the prolarva is lecithotrophic, subsisting entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves while it undergoes rapid organogenesis and retinal differentiation. The first exogenous feeding event typically occurs within three to five days post-hatching, coinciding with the completion of yolk absorption and the opening of the mouth gape, at which point the larva begins to capture small copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. The progression from yolk dependency to active feeding represents a critical period of high mortality, as individuals that fail to locate suitable prey within the window of yolk reserve depletion experience irreversible starvation.

As the Largescale blackfish progresses through its life cycle, it undergoes a substantial increase in body mass that culminates in the attainment of its ultimate wet weight. The maximum recorded adult body mass in this species is approximately 3,170 grams [Wwi = approximately 3,170 grams], a value derived from the terminal length of 50 centimeters through application of the species-specific length-weight relationship. This ultimate mass represents the asymptotic body size beyond which further somatic investment becomes negligible, with individuals shifting all surplus energy toward gamete production and spawning activities. The growth trajectory from the 0.0009 gram birth mass to the 3,170 gram adult mass spans several orders of magnitude and reflects a relatively slow, sustained growth rate characteristic of a temperate, iteroparous species that invests in multiple reproductive bouts across its lifespan. The time to reach sexual maturity is approximately 2 years after hatching [tp = 2 years after hatching], marking the transition from somatic growth to reproductive investment. Comparative data from related kyphosid fishes indicate that Girella punctata occupies an intermediate position in terms of terminal body size, being smaller than the larger Girella elevata but exceeding the dimensions of more diminutive congeners such as Girella zebra from Australian waters.

Lifespan data for the Largescale blackfish indicate that individuals can achieve considerable longevity under natural conditions when mortality from predation and fishing is low. The time since birth at death, based on age estimations from otolith annuli analysis and validated by captive rearing experiments conducted at a water temperature of 22.4 °C [T = 22.4 °C], is approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years]. This lifespan places the species among the longer-lived members of the Kyphosidae, a pattern that is consistent with its moderate body size and iteroparous life history characterized by deferred maturity and repeated reproductive events. The longevity of 13 years allows individuals to accumulate multiple spawning seasons, thereby increasing the probability of recruiting offspring during years when oceanographic conditions favor larval survival and settlement. From a population perspective, this extended reproductive window functions as a buffer against sporadic recruitment failures, a common feature in the life histories of temperate marine fishes that inhabit environmentally variable coastal ecosystems.
